intro: Look up from ground level and trace how the structure directs your eye.
alt: Four architectural settings show stone columns, pointed vaults, a patterned courtyard and a cellular vault.

variants.name: Classical orders
variants.look: Columns and capitals carry an entablature at regular intervals.
variants.history: Greek and Roman traditions established distinct systems of column proportion, capital and entablature later codified in architectural treatises.
variants.when: Read a classical façade by comparing the proportions and profiles from base to cornice.
variants.why: Distinct capital profiles and column-to-entablature ratios make orders recognizable across buildings.

source.label: The Met · Architecture in Ancient Greece

variants.name: Gothic cathedral architecture
variants.look: Pointed arches and clustered piers guide the eye into a ribbed canopy.
variants.history: Gothic builders combined pointed arches, rib vaults and buttressing to construct taller interiors and larger windows.
variants.when: Trace where the web of ribs meets the piers to see how the interior is organized.
variants.why: The meeting of the ribs and piers turns engineering into a repeated visual cue.
variants.period: From the mid-12th century in France

variants.name: Islamic architecture
variants.look: An arcade and patterned surfaces organize a courtyard around space and light.
variants.history: Architecture across Islamic societies developed many local traditions, including courtyard, garden, mosque and palace types.
variants.when: Identify spatial organization and regional materials alongside ornament.
variants.why: Courtyard axes and arcades choreograph movement, shade and moments of stillness.

source.label: The Met · The Nature of Islamic Art

variants.name: muqarnas
variants.look: Repeated niches break the curve overhead into small, layered cells.
variants.history: Muqarnas developed in medieval Islamic architecture and is used under domes and cornices and above portals.
variants.when: Study connected tiers to see how builders mediate between flat walls and curved or polygonal spaces.
variants.why: Tiered cells make a transition between two larger shapes perceptible in small steps.

source.label: The Met · Panel from a Ceiling

prompt: Draw a single textless art comparison board for a museum-quality online art atlas. Layout is exactly four square cells in 2x2, edge-to-edge, no gutters or borders; precise, strictly equally sized cells. Order is left to right within each row, then next row. Each cell is a distinct style treatment featuring the same female executive from reference, in original new art. The reference image is for identity only: recognizable ash-blonde hair in neat low bun with four-color windowpane hair clip, black-rimmed rectangular glasses over blue eyes, charcoal sheath dress under fitted black blazer, azure pocket square and blue lanyard with blank ID badge, holding a white coffee mug with a little four-color tile mark. Change the actual render style rather than adding only backgrounds. Layout styles in order: Classical orders: executive standing by rhythmic stone columns with distinct capitals and measured entablature in clear limestone daylight; Gothic cathedral architecture: executive dwarfed by pointed arches, rib vaults, vertical piers and stained light; Islamic architecture: executive centered in a tranquil garden court with tiled geometric wall, rhythm of arches and reflecting pool; muqarnas: low angle on executive looking up with mug to cellular three-dimensional niches which step into a vault, turquoise and honey stone. No readable text, numbers, signatures, words, or extra panels.
